opening.headline: Learn where and how to store your preferences to remember them even after a session.
body: Yesterday, a user asked me to give a short answer in Korean and without a table. But when I open a new session today, the agent has no idea about this preference. This is because the context window only lives within one conversation, and information that goes out of the window disappears.

In this class, we look at the structure of external memory, which leaves information beyond conversations. Compare Claude's memory tools, Google's Memory Bank, and ADK's memory services, and practice distinguishing between session state and long-term memory to determine what to put where. The risk of personal information remaining in memory is also covered as an example.

Distinguish between session state and long-term memory

paragraphs: Yesterday, the user told the agent, "Give me a short answer in Korean and without a ticket." The agent complied with the request and the conversation ended satisfactorily.

Today, when a user opened a new session and asked a question, the agent responded with a lengthy table in English. Because we have no idea what yesterday’s preferences were. The user must provide the same explanation again.

A context window only lives within a conversation. When a conversation ends and a new session starts, the contents of the previous window are not passed on to the model. The model itself does not remember what it heard in the conversation.
So where, who, and how should we keep what we need to remember even after the session is over? This lesson covers three structures to answer that question.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Would it be possible to save all conversations and paste them into the next session? We'll come back to this question at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let me think about whether I have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think back: The moment you explained it from the beginning every time
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced repeating the same background information over and over again with each new conversation?
items.answer: Many people go through this. This is not a performance issue with the agent, but rather its structure. Since each conversation opens a new context window, remembering requires a mechanism to store information outside the window and retrieve it when needed.

items.prompt: When has there been a moment when you wish your agent would have remembered a decision or lesson from a previous job?
items.answer: Examples include user preferences, project rules, and lessons learned from past work. Once this information is set, it is used repeatedly in multiple sessions, so it is good to keep in long-term memory.

items.prompt: Was there a scene where you felt uncomfortable remembering information you shouldn't?
items.answer: Memory is both an advantage and a risk. If personal, temporary or incorrect information is stored, it will continue to affect future sessions. So the policy of deciding what to remember is as important as the storage technology.

screens.outro: Now that we have organized our experience, let us first distinguish between short-term memory and long-term memory.

screens.title: Distinction between session state and long-term memory
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the scope and nature of session and long-term memory.

visual.alt: Schematic showing how session state resides within a conversation and long-term memory is retrieved across multiple sessions.

states.label: Session state (short-term memory)
states.body: ADK's Session is a short-term memory that contains event records and temporary data (state) of one conversation. It contains values ​​that are necessary for the progress of the current conversation, such as what stage it is at and the preferences set in this conversation. This is suitable for information that can be discarded at the end of a conversation. The model only sees what is contained in the current window.

states.label: long term memory
states.body: MemoryService is a long-term, searchable knowledge repository containing information from multiple past conversations. Keep facts to keep in mind after the conversation is over, such as the user's language and format preferences or conclusions from past work. Rather than loading all of the long-term memory, only the pieces needed are retrieved through searches such as search_memory. Saving and retrieving must be designed separately. When you mix the two, temporary values ​​clutter your long-term memory, or long-lasting preferences get lost along with the conversation. In the cognitive structural model that studies agent memory, long-term memory is divided into facts and knowledge (semantic), records of past experiences (episodic), and methods of action (procedural). The user's language preference is closer to facts, the conclusion of past work is closer to experience, and repeated work procedures are closer to methods. Knowing this distinction will give you a baseline when choosing what to store.

screens.outro: Now that you know the distinction, let's see step-by-step how Claude's memory tool works.

ext.title: Sumers et al., Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (2023)

screens.title: Flow of memory tools reading and writing files
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to step through the order in which memory tool calls occur.

steps.title: Check the directory before starting the task
steps.body: The memory tool creates, reads, modifies, and deletes files in the /memories directory, maintaining information between sessions. Before Claude starts working, he first checks the memory directory with the view command. This is to see if there are any records left from previous sessions.

steps.title: Claude asks for orders
steps.body: Available commands are view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, rename. When Claude wants to record preferences, for example, he asks create to create a file under /memories. In this case, Claude only makes a request and does not create the file directly.

steps.title: My application performs actual operations
steps.body: Memory tools are client-side tools. My application performs the actual file reading and writing, and returns the results to Claude as tool_result. My code decides where to store it and whose records it is.

steps.title: I control the storage location and scope
steps.body: The storage location, for example a user-specific folder or database key, is determined by my infrastructure. All operations should be restricted to /memories. Failure to verify the path may result in problems reading or overwriting files in other locations.

steps.title: Read again next session
steps.body: In a new session, when Claude checks the directory again with view, he sees the file he left yesterday, reads its contents, and brings it into context. This preference continues even if the session changes. The content you read takes up context, so dividing the file into small, topical pieces makes it easier to read only what you need.

screens.outro: Let's look at the following structure, remembering that Claude only makes requests and the application handles storage.

screens.title: Keyword search and embedding similarity search
screens.lead: Read the table to compare the methods and limitations of the two search methods for finding memories. The explanation below the table also explains what embedding is.

visual.alt: A two-dimensional diagram in which sentences with close meaning are grouped together in a vector space.
labels: Even English documents are explained in Korean.
Payment is processed at the end of the month

data.caption: Two ways to search for memories (hypothetical examples: memory 'User prefers answers in Korean', question 'What word should I answer?')
rows: How to save
Store memory sentences verbatim and index them so you can find them by word.
Convert the memory sentence into an embedding vector, a list of numbers containing meaning, and store it with the sentence.
How to handle questions
Make sure the words in the question are still in your memory.
Convert the questions into vectors in the same way, and choose the memory with the closest vector.
Example results
This memory cannot be found because there are no words that overlap between the question and the memory.
I look for this memory because the meanings of 'answer' and 'response', 'word' and 'Korean' are close.
strengths
Simple and predictable when looking for identifiers or proper nouns that require the word to match exactly.
Even if the expressions are different, if the meaning is similar, you can find it, so it is suitable for finding natural language preferences or facts.
limit
Other expressions with the same meaning are missed.
Since it is a method of selecting something close, even if you don't have any related memories, you can retrieve the relatively closest random memory.
data.notes: Embedding is a method of converting a sentence into a vector of hundreds of numbers or more. The model that creates this is trained so that sentences with similar meanings are vectors that are close together. How close two vectors are is measured by a value such as cosine similarity. Similarity search does not find an exact match, but rather returns the top few closest matches. Therefore, imported memories should be treated as candidates rather than established facts. Which memories are returned depends on the baseline settings, so it's safe to design designs that limit the number, narrow them by scope, and check the current conversation one more time before taking important actions.

screens.outro: Now that you know the principles of search, let's look at services that create memories from conversations and even provide searches.

screens.title: Memory Bank: A service that creates memories from conversations
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Memory Bank is a service that dynamically generates long-term memory through interactions between users and agents, maintaining it across multiple sessions. Each memory contains a single independent fact and is stored in a collection separated by scope. Memory extraction extracts only meaningful information from conversations, while Synthesis combines new information with existing memories to update them. GenerateMemories automatically retrieves memories into extraction, and CreateMemory allows the agent to directly write memories. RetrieveMemories retrieves either the entire memory set or only related memories via similarity search and inserts them into prompts. This enables the agent to maintain context without requiring the user to repeatedly restate preferences.

terms.tip: This is the standard for separating memories. Divide the collection by values ​​such as agent name or user ID to avoid mixing up other users' memories.
This is a step where only meaningful information is extracted as independent facts, rather than storing the entire conversation.
This is the stage where newly collected information is combined with existing memories and updated. Reduce duplicate or conflicting content.
This is a call that automatically extracts and creates memories from conversations.
A call in which an agent or application directly writes a memory.
It is a call to retrieve stored memories. Import everything, or select and import only relevant memories using similarity search.

screens.outro: Now that we have seen memory in the form of a service, let us compare the implementation provided by ADK and the write/read policy.

screens.title: ADK memory and memory write/retrieval policy
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about ADK's memory implementation and storage/retrieval policy.

tabs.label: InMemoryMemoryService
tabs.body: This is an implementation for prototyping. The data is lost when the application restarts, and searches are based on keyword matches. It's great for quickly confirming concepts, but it's not good for long-term memory of actual services.

tabs.label: VertexAiMemoryBankService
tabs.body: It is an implementation that creates evolving memories by extracting meaningful information from conversations. This is a method of using Memory Bank in ADK, and when new information comes in, it is updated by integrating it with existing memories. It is suitable for information that will be retained for a long time, such as user-specific preferences.

tabs.label: VertexAiRagMemoryService
tabs.body: This is an implementation for recovering the entire conversation using vector search. It is used when you need to revisit the original context of the conversation rather than summarized facts. The difference, unlike extract-based implementations, is that the units stored are larger.

tabs.label: write policy
tabs.body: What to remember is determined by the writing policy. add_session_to_memory adds the entire session, add_events_to_memory selects only some events, and add_memory adds items directly. If you add an entire session, it will also pile up simple but unnecessary content.

tabs.label: read policy
tabs.body: When reading, the agent retrieves it at the moment of need using tools like load_memory. Since only the pieces matching the query are retrieved rather than loading all of the long-term memory into the context, the problem of the context growing unnecessarily is also reduced.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at the structure, let's solve the risk case step by step.

screens.title: Explanatory example: When personal information remains in memory
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: A flow diagram in which information extracted from a conversation is filtered and stored.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Customer support agents automatically extract names, contact information, and health information from conversations and store them in long-term memory. This design started with good intentions to reduce user inconvenience.

steps.title: Step 1: Regardless of whether you are sensitive or not
steps.body: Automatic extraction only extracts meaningful information and does not determine whether the information is sensitive. Your health information will also be stored unless you specifically block it.

steps.title: Stage 2: Revived in the wrong place
steps.body: Several months later, another session retrieves this memory, pulling personal information unrelated to the question into the response. Users become frustrated when they see information they didn't know they remembered.

steps.title: Step 3: False information becomes fact
steps.body: When something malicious or incorrect is stored as a memory in a conversation, subsequent sessions will believe it to be true and act on it. This is called memory poisoning. Once saved, it affects multiple sessions. OWASP's Agent Threat Guide also addresses memory corruption as one of the threats agents face. Unlike a one-time input error, it is characterized by remaining in the storage and repeatedly affecting it.

steps.title: Why is it so hard to notice
steps.body: This risk is not normally apparent. When memory is working well, the user experience is better, so you don't check your saves, and problems show up months later at random moments. Therefore, a filtering policy at the storage stage and a path for humans to review the stored content are needed. Your design should also include features that allow users to view and clear their memories.

steps.title: response
steps.body: Limit the topics to be saved and isolate each user using scope. Sensitive information is excluded from storage and mitigation measures such as Model Armor and human review are in place. Storage is checked separately with the write policy, and retrieval is checked with the search policy. Even when an agent acts based on a memory it has read, if the action is important, it is safer to have it double-checked in the current conversation rather than relying solely on the memory.

screens.outro: Now that you understand the risks, let’s table the criteria for what to remember and what to forget.

data.notes: Storage is designed separately as a write policy, and retrieval as a search policy. Even if the same information is filtered out in the write, it cannot be found in the search, and even if it is allowed in the write, the scope can be narrowed in the search stage. Both steps must be checked to be safe. Also, since the same information may be judged differently depending on the purpose of the service, use the standards in the table as a starting point and adjust them to suit your service. Part of the design is to let users know what information is being stored and to allow them to erase it. Keeping these criteria in a team document allows you to repeat the same judgments each time you create a new feature. If you read the rows of the table by dividing them into facts, experiences, and methods, you can see that preferences and rules are closer to facts, and lessons from past work are closer to experiences. Having a breakdown makes it easier to explain which items to save and which to leave in the session or discard.

screens.outro: I will gather the analysis and summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Expand items to see evidence
screens.lead: When you select each item, the basis for the summary statement will unfold. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.title: Short-term memory is handled by the session state, and long-term memory is handled by memory services or memory files.
items.body: Session state contains temporary values needed to proceed with a conversation, and long-term memory contains facts that will be used even after the conversation ends. Long-term memory retrieves only the pieces it needs by searching. The first design principle is not to mix the two memories. Once a distinction is made, it must be shared within the team using the same words.

items.title: The memory tool handles requests from Claude and storage from my application.
items.body: Memory tools are client-side tools. Claude requests a command, and my application returns a result by manipulating the actual files in /memories.

items.title: Memory Bank extracts and integrates facts from conversations and isolates them by scope.
items.body: Each memory is an independent fact and is kept in a scope-specific collection. Automatically extract with GenerateMemories or write directly with CreateMemory, and retrieve only the memories you need with RetrieveMemories. You can choose the method that suits your situation: the whole method or the similarity search method.

items.title: Memory write policy and privacy control are key to long-term memory design.
items.body: What you store and what you block determines the quality and safety of your memories. Design controls such as exclusion of sensitive information, isolation by user, and human moderation along with write policies. It also includes a path that allows users to view and delete saved information.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this lesson are memory tools, Memory Bank, long-term memory, and memory retrieval. Let's go back to the first question. Would it be possible to save all conversations and paste them into the next session?

Doing so quickly fills up the context window, bringing with it unnecessary or sensitive information. A much better structure is to extract and store only the necessary facts and retrieve them through search when needed.

If I'm creating an agent, I can first list out what information needs to remain after the session ends. As this list gets longer, it becomes important to distinguish between what needs to be saved and what needs to be retrieved. Next, consider whether each item belongs to session state, user-scoped long-term memory, or information that you don't want to store.

Also, we need to design how and who can correct or delete the stored information if it is incorrect. In other words, it is also subject to check whether the information the user requested to be erased actually disappears. The path to correcting and erasing memories is as important as the function of creating memories. Without this path, one bad save will linger for a long time.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: Where do I get stuck with memory tools in my work? Think about the information you want to remember and the information you don't want to remember, and think about where to put each.

checks.q: Who actually reads and writes files in the memory tool (/memories directory)?
options: Claude creates files directly inside the server
Anthropic automatically operates repositories for each user
Since it is a client-side tool, my application performs it and returns it as tool_result.
The Memory Bank service handles it for you.
checks.explain: The memory tool is a client-side tool, so Claude only makes requests. My infrastructure is responsible for storage locations and restrictions within /memories.

wrong.0: Claude only requests commands and does not directly manipulate files.
wrong.1: The storage location is determined by my infrastructure.
wrong.3: Memory Bank is a separate service and has a different structure from the memory tool.

checks.intro: Check out the memory tool to see who is actually reading and writing your files.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The memory tool is a client-side tool, so Claude just makes the request and my application does it.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It would be wrong to think that a server or separate service stores it. Remember that the memory tool is client-side, so the storage location and /memories range limits are up to you.

checks.q: Match the following memory implementations and features:
right: Create evolving memories by extracting meaningful information from conversations
This is a writing method that selects only some events of the session and stores them in memory.
The purpose is to retrieve the entire conversation using vector search.
It is for prototyping and disappears when restarted and is searched by keyword match.
checks.explain: Each implementation has different persistence and retrieval methods. add_events_to_memory is a write policy that remembers only a portion of the service, not the service.
checks.intro: Each memory implementation has different storage and retrieval methods. Match implementations and features.
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. You distinguished implementations by persistence and retrieval methods, and also pointed out that add_events_to_memory is a write policy.
checks.incorrectFeedback: More than one pair was misaligned. Let's break it down into a prototype that disappears when restarted, a Memory Bank that extracts information, and a RAG method that finds and attaches related content using vector search, and confirm that add_events_to_memory is a writing method, not a service.

checks.q: The customer support agent addresses the preference of ‘please answer briefly in Korean’ and ‘current payment progress stage’. What is the appropriate location for both pieces of information?
options: It is safe to store both preference and progression steps in long-term memory.
Preference is given to user-scoped long-term memory, with progress placed in session state.
Preference is given to session state, with progress steps placed in user-scoped long-term memory.
Neither is saved and the user is asked again each time.
checks.explain: User-scoped long-term memory is good because preferences such as language and format are needed even after the session ends. The current work progress is placed in a session state that can be discarded once the conversation is over.

wrong.0: If you store it for a long time until the advanced stage, unnecessary information accumulates, increasing the burden of search and personal information.
wrong.2: If a preference is only in session state, it will be lost in the new session.
wrong.3: Asking for preferences every time that must be remembered even after the session is over does not solve this problem.

checks.intro: The two pieces of information have different lifetimes. Decide where you should place each.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Even after a session ends, necessary preferences are kept in user-scoped long-term memory, and the progress of the current task is kept in session state.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Information should be divided based on its lifespan. When a conversation ends, values ​​that can be discarded are session state, and values ​​that are needed for the next conversation are long-term memory.

glossary.def: Claude's client-side tool that creates, reads, and modifies files in the /memories directory and maintains information between sessions.
This is a service of the Google agent platform that extracts and integrates facts from conversations and manages them as long-term memory by scope.
It is a repository that remains after the session ends and can be retrieved across multiple conversations. ADK's MemoryService is an example.
This is a read action that takes only the memories you need into the query and puts them into the prompt.
The risk is that false information will be stored in memory and subsequent sessions will act accordingly.

This is a search that converts sentences into vectors containing meaning and searches for memories of vectors that are close to the question. Even if the words are different, if they have similar meanings, you will find them, but they may bring up strange memories.

misconceptions.myth: Session state and long-term memory are the same.
misconceptions.fact: State is a temporary partition of a conversation, while long-term memory is a repository that can be retrieved across conversations.

misconceptions.myth: The memory tool saves files directly from Claude.
misconceptions.fact: Memory tools are client-side tools. Claude just makes the request and my application does the actual saving.

misconceptions.myth: You can trust all your stored memories.
misconceptions.fact: False or sensitive information may be stored. Write and search policies and isolation per user are required.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Short-term memory is handled by the session state, and long-term memory is handled by the memory service or memory file.
The memory tool handles requests from Claude and storage from my application.
Memory Bank extracts facts from conversations, consolidates them, and isolates them by scope.
Memory write policy and privacy control are key to long-term memory design.
